o: Representing the UK to the rest of the world

q: At the State Opening of Parliament, what does the monarch's speech set out?
e: The monarch makes a speech summarising the government's policies for the year ahead.
o: The government's policies for the next session
The results of the general election
The rates of tax for the coming year

q: The monarch has the right to be consulted, to encourage and to warn the government.
e: True. The monarch has regular meetings with the Prime Minister and can advise, warn and encourage.

q: The monarch is the head of the Commonwealth.
e: True. The monarch is the ceremonial head of the Commonwealth.

q: What are the two Houses of Parliament?
e: Parliament has two Houses: the House of Commons and the House of Lords.
o: The House of Commons and the House of Lords
The House of Commons and the Senate
The House of Lords and the Supreme Court
The House of Commons and the Cabinet

q: Which House of Parliament is the more important chamber?
e: The House of Commons is regarded as the more important of the two chambers because its members are democratically elected.

q: What are the people elected to the House of Commons called?
e: The people elected to the House of Commons are Members of Parliament (MPs).

q: What is the area that each MP represents called?
e: Each MP represents a parliamentary constituency.

q: How many parliamentary constituencies are there in the UK?
e: The UK is divided into 650 parliamentary constituencies, each electing one MP.

q: How often must a general election be held?
e: General elections are held at least every five years.

q: What happens if an MP dies or resigns?
e: If an MP dies or resigns, there is a by-election in their constituency.
o: The party appoints a new MP
The monarch appoints a new MP

q: Which electoral system is used to elect MPs?
e: MPs are elected through a system called "first past the post". The candidate with the most votes wins.

q: What do party whips do?
e: Whips are responsible for discipline in their party and for making sure MPs attend the House of Commons to vote.
o: Ensure discipline and attendance at votes
Chair debates in the House of Commons
Write the text of new laws

q: Who chairs debates in the House of Commons?
e: Debates in the House of Commons are chaired by the Speaker, who keeps order.

q: How is the Speaker of the House of Commons chosen?
e: The Speaker is chosen by other MPs in a secret ballot.
o: By MPs in a secret ballot

q: The Speaker of the House of Commons is politically neutral.
e: True. The Speaker is neutral but still represents a constituency as an MP.

q: Members of the House of Lords are elected by the public.
e: False. Members of the House of Lords, known as peers, are not elected by the people.

q: Since 1958, who has had the power to nominate life peers?
e: Since 1958 the Prime Minister has had the power to nominate peers just for their own lifetime.

q: Which TWO groups can sit in the House of Lords?
e: The House of Lords includes life peers, some hereditary peers and senior bishops of the Church of England.
o: Senior bishops of the Church of England

q: What can the House of Lords do with new laws proposed by the House of Commons?
e: The House of Lords checks laws passed by the House of Commons and can suggest amendments or propose new laws.
o: Put them to a public vote
Send them to the monarch to decide

q: The House of Commons has powers to overrule the House of Lords.
e: True. The House of Commons can overrule the House of Lords, but these powers are not used often.

q: Where is the Prime Minister's official home?
e: The Prime Minister's official home is 10 Downing Street, in central London.

q: What is the name of the Prime Minister's country house?
e: The Prime Minister also has a country house outside London called Chequers.

q: Who is usually the Prime Minister?
e: The Prime Minister is the leader of the political party in power.
o: The leader of the governing party
The leader of the House of Lords
The Speaker of the House of Commons

q: What is the Cabinet?
e: The Prime Minister appoints about 20 senior MPs to become ministers in charge of departments. These ministers form the Cabinet.
o: All MPs in the governing party
A committee of the House of Lords

q: Which Cabinet minister is responsible for the economy?
e: The Chancellor of the Exchequer is responsible for the economy.

q: Which Cabinet minister is responsible for crime, policing and immigration?
e: The Home Secretary is responsible for crime, policing and immigration.

q: Which Cabinet minister manages the UK's relationship with other countries?
e: The Foreign Secretary manages relationships with foreign countries.

q: Which party forms the Official Opposition?
e: The second-largest party in the House of Commons is called the Opposition.
o: The second-largest party in the Commons
The largest party in the House of Lords
The party with the most councillors

q: What does the Leader of the Opposition appoint?
e: The Leader of the Opposition appoints senior opposition MPs to be "shadow ministers", who form the shadow cabinet.

q: Who leads the questioning of the Prime Minister at Prime Minister's Questions?
e: The Leader of the Opposition leads the questioning of the Prime Minister on issues of the day.

q: How often does Prime Minister's Questions take place while Parliament is sitting?
e: Prime Minister's Questions takes place every week while Parliament is sitting.

q: What are pressure and lobby groups?
e: Pressure and lobby groups are organisations which try to influence government policy.
o: Groups that try to influence government policy
Committees of MPs that review laws
Groups of judges who advise Parliament

q: Civil servants are politically neutral.
e: True. Civil servants are chosen on merit and are politically neutral.

q: Who carries out government policy?
e: Civil servants support the government in developing and implementing its policies.
o: Members of the House of Lords

q: Which of these services do local authorities provide?
e: Local authorities provide services such as education, housing, social services, refuse collection and libraries.

q: In which month are most local elections held?
e: Most local authority elections are held in May every year.

q: Some towns and cities have a directly elected mayor.
e: True. Many towns and cities, including London, have a directly elected mayor.

q: Since 1997, some powers have been given to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. What is this called?
e: Since 1997, some powers have been devolved from central government to give people more control over matters that directly affect them.

q: Where does the Scottish Parliament sit?
e: The Scottish Parliament sits in Edinburgh, at Holyrood.

q: How are members of the Scottish Parliament (MSPs) elected?
e: MSPs are elected by a form of proportional representation.
o: By first past the post only

q: Where is the Welsh Senedd building?
e: The Welsh Parliament meets in the Senedd building in Cardiff Bay.
x: The Welsh Assembly has been called the Senedd (Welsh Parliament) since 2020.

q: Where does the Northern Ireland Assembly meet?
e: The Northern Ireland Assembly meets at Stormont, in Belfast.

q: Which agreement led to the setting up of the Northern Ireland Assembly?
e: The Northern Ireland Assembly was established soon after the Belfast (Good Friday) Agreement in 1998.

q: The Northern Ireland Assembly has been suspended on several occasions.
e: True. The UK government has the power to suspend the Assembly if political leaders cannot agree.

q: What is the name of the official report of proceedings in Parliament?
e: Proceedings in Parliament are published in official reports called Hansard.

q: The press in the UK is free from government control.
e: True. The UK has a free press. Owners and editors may hold strong political opinions.

q: By law, radio and television coverage of political parties must be balanced.
e: True. Coverage of political parties must give equal time to rival viewpoints.

q: What is the minimum age to vote in UK Parliament elections?
e: The present voting age of 18 was set in 1969.
x: In Scotland and Wales, people can vote at 16 in some elections. For the test, use the handbook's answer.

q: Apart from UK citizens, which TWO groups can vote in all UK public elections if they are resident here and aged 18 or over?
e: Adult citizens of the UK, and citizens of the Commonwealth and the Irish Republic who are resident in the UK, can vote in all public elections.

q: What must you do before you can vote?
e: To be able to vote you must have your name on the electoral register.
o: Pass a test about the UK's politics
Join a political party in your area
Pay a fee to your local council

q: Where can you register to vote?
e: You can register online or by contacting your local council's electoral registration office.
o: Online or through your local council
Only at your MP's local office
At a polling station on election day

q: Where do people vote in person in elections?
e: People vote in elections at places called polling stations, or polling places in Scotland.

q: What are the opening hours of polling stations on election day?
e: On election day the polling station is open from 7 am until 10 pm.

q: You can apply to vote by post instead of going to a polling station.
e: True. If it is difficult for you to get to a polling station, you can register for a postal ballot.

q: Your vote is secret, and no one can make you say who you voted for.
e: True. Voting is done in secret.

q: Which TWO groups of people cannot stand for election as an MP?
e: Most citizens aged 18 or over can stand. Exceptions include members of the armed forces, civil servants and people found guilty of certain criminal offences.

q: How can you meet your MP in person?
e: Many MPs hold regular local "surgeries", which are often advertised in the local newspaper.
o: At one of their local surgeries

q: Members of the public can watch debates in the Houses of Parliament.
e: True. The public can watch from the public galleries. Entrance is free.

q: What is the Commonwealth?
e: The Commonwealth is an association of countries that support each other and work together. Most were once part of the British Empire.
o: A trading group of European countries

q: What did the Council of Europe create?
e: The Council of Europe is separate from the EU. It developed the European Convention on Human Rights.
o: The European Convention on Human Rights

q: Which international organisation was set up after the Second World War to prevent war and promote international peace?
e: The United Nations (UN) was set up after the Second World War. The UK is a member.

q: The UK is one of how many permanent members of the UN Security Council?
e: The UK is one of five permanent members of the UN Security Council.

q: What do NATO members agree to do?
e: NATO is a group of European and North American countries that have agreed to help each other if attacked.
o: Help each other if they are attacked

q: Which TWO are examples of criminal offences?
e: Carrying a weapon and selling tobacco to anyone under 18 are crimes. Disputes about goods and housing are civil matters.

q: Which TWO are examples of civil law?
e: Civil law is used to settle disputes between individuals or groups, such as consumer rights, housing and employment.

q: It is a criminal offence to smoke in almost every enclosed public place in the UK.
e: True. It is against the law to smoke in almost every enclosed public place.

q: It is legal to buy alcohol for someone under 18.
e: False. It is a criminal offence to buy alcohol for people under 18.

q: What is the minimum age at which you can buy tobacco products?
e: It is a criminal offence to sell tobacco products to anyone under 18.
x: Tobacco laws are changing so that people born on or after 1 January 2009 may never be sold tobacco. Check GOV.UK.

q: Which TWO are duties of the police?
e: The police protect life and property, prevent disturbances, and prevent and detect crime.

q: Who supports the police by patrolling the streets?
e: Police community support officers (PCSOs) patrol the streets and work with the public.

q: Since 2012, who have people in England and Wales elected to ensure the police are effective?
e: In November 2012, the public elected Police and Crime Commissioners (PCCs) in England and Wales.
x: The government has announced plans to replace PCCs. For the test, use the handbook's answer.

q: The police must obey the law and must not misuse their authority.
e: True. The police are servants of the public and must act within the law.

q: Who usually hears minor criminal cases in England, Wales and Northern Ireland?
e: Most minor criminal cases are dealt with in a magistrates' court.

q: Magistrates are usually paid and must have legal qualifications.
e: False. Magistrates usually work unpaid and do not need legal qualifications. They receive training.

q: Where are serious criminal offences tried in England, Wales and Northern Ireland?
e: Serious offences are tried in front of a judge and a jury in a Crown Court.

q: How many people are on a jury in England, Wales and Northern Ireland?
e: A jury in England, Wales and Northern Ireland has 12 members.

q: How many people are on a jury in Scotland?
e: In Scotland a jury has 15 members.

q: In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, which court hears cases against young people aged 10 to 17?
e: If an accused person is aged 10 to 17, the case is normally heard in a youth court.

q: What system does Scotland use to deal with children and young people accused of an offence?
e: Scotland has a system called the Children's Hearings System.

q: In England and Wales, which court deals with civil disputes such as debts and personal injury?
e: County Courts deal with a wide range of civil disputes.

q: What is the small claims procedure?
e: The small claims procedure is an informal way of helping people to settle minor disputes without spending a lot of money on a lawyer.
o: An informal way to settle minor disputes
A criminal court for minor theft

q: In a criminal trial, the jury decides whether the accused is guilty or not guilty.
e: True. If the accused is found guilty, the judge decides the penalty.

q: Which law brought most of the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law?
e: Most of the Convention's articles have been incorporated into UK law through the Human Rights Act 1998.

q: Which TWO rights are protected by the European Convention on Human Rights?
e: The Convention includes the right to life, a fair trial, freedom from torture, and freedom of thought, conscience and religion.
o: Freedom of thought, conscience and religion

q: Which law protects people from discrimination in England, Wales and Scotland?
e: The Equality Act 2010 makes it illegal to discriminate in a wide range of areas, including work and public services.

q: Violence towards a partner, whether married or not, is a serious crime.
e: True. Anyone who is violent towards their partner can be prosecuted.

q: Female genital mutilation (FGM) is a crime in the UK.
e: True. It is a criminal offence to carry out FGM or to arrange for it to be carried out.

q: What is a forced marriage?
e: A forced marriage is where one or both parties do not or cannot give their consent. It is a criminal offence.
o: A marriage without the consent of both people
A marriage arranged with both people's consent
A marriage that takes place abroad
A marriage at a register office

q: An arranged marriage, where both people agree, is the same as a forced marriage.
e: False. In an arranged marriage both people agree. A forced marriage is without their consent and is illegal.

q: Which of these do you pay income tax on?
e: Income tax is paid on wages, profits from self-employment, taxable benefits, pensions and income from property and savings.

q: How is income tax usually paid by people who work for an employer?
e: For most people, tax is deducted automatically from their pay through a system called Pay As You Earn (PAYE).

q: Who must pay their own tax through self assessment?
e: People who are self-employed need to pay their own tax through a system called self assessment.

q: What are National Insurance contributions used for?
e: National Insurance contributions pay for state benefits and services such as the State Pension and the NHS.

q: Almost everybody in the UK who is in paid work, including self-employed people, must pay National Insurance contributions.
e: True. People who do not pay enough may not receive certain benefits or a full State Pension.

q: What is the minimum age at which you can drive a car in the UK?
e: You must be at least 17 years old to drive a car or motorcycle.

q: What happens to your driving licence when you reach 70?
e: A driving licence is valid until you are 70. After that it is valid for three years at a time.
o: You must renew it every three years
You must take a new driving test

q: It is a criminal offence to drive without insurance.
e: True. All drivers must have insurance.

q: What must cars over three years old pass every year?
e: If your vehicle is over three years old, it must have a Ministry of Transport (MOT) test every year.

q: Volunteering is a good way to support your local community.
e: True. Volunteering and working with your community is a good way to support it.

q: Which TWO are good ways to help protect the environment?
e: Recycling, walking or using public transport, and buying local products help protect the environment.
o: Using a car for short journeys

q: Dropping litter in the street can result in a fine.
e: True. It is a criminal offence to drop litter.

q: Who may be asked to serve on a jury?
e: Anyone on the electoral register may be chosen at random to serve on a jury.

q: Anyone on the electoral register may be asked to serve on a jury.
e: True. People on the electoral register can be chosen at random. Some people cannot serve.

q: How can parents help their children's school?
e: Parents can become school governors (school board members in Scotland).

q: You can register to become an organ donor.
e: True. You can register to donate your organs after you die.
x: Across the UK, most adults are now treated as donors unless they opt out.

q: Which number can you call in an emergency for police, fire or ambulance?
e: In an emergency call 999 or 112.

q: What does the national anthem ask God to do for the monarch?
e: The national anthem is "God Save the King".

q: It is legal for a man to force his wife to have sex.
e: False. It is a crime for any man to force a woman to have sex, including his wife.

q: Which of these is a way to take part in politics?
e: You can join a political party, help with campaigns or stand for office.

q: Members of the public can visit the Scottish Parliament, the Senedd and the Northern Ireland Assembly.
e: True. You can get information about visiting from each of them.
